newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish Oct credit growth rate seen rising - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Irish Oct credit growth rate seen rising - analysts.

text.p: While Irish private sector credit growth is expected to reflect continuing strength in the economy when the central bank publishes its end-October statistics on Thursday, it is not expected to lead to a near-term rise in interest rates, economists believe.
Some economists see Irish private-sector credit growth as high as 14 percent at end-October compared with 13.3 percent at end-September.
A booming construction sector is expected to push residential mortgage lending growth rates close to 17 percent from 16.5 percent at end-September.
"We are going for credit growth of 14 percent," Goodbody Stockbrokers economist Jenny Pollock told Reuters.
"For the mortgage number, we still see it growing strongly and expect it to creep up to 16.8 percent this time from 16.5 percent in September."

Pollock said that even it the credit figures bounced as vigourously as she was predicting she did not think it would lead to the central bank putting up interest rates, at least not in the short term.
"But while we are not expecting a panic reaction I am sure the market would be happier with a lower number than we are projecting," she added.
NCB economist Eunan King forecast credit growth of 13.5 percent while Riada Stockbrokers expect the number to be at or around last month's level of 13.3 percent.
"We are going for 13.5 percent (credit growth) but 14 percent seems to be around the market and we do not have any grounds for disagreeing strongly with that," King said.

Riada economist Padraic Garvey said the fact that Ireland had some weak retail sales numbers recently may indicate a certain amount of slowdown in the economy and on that basis he expected the figure to remain close to last month's level.

"There is of course a possibility that there will be a spike-back from September's numbers which were remarkably weak, and if there is, I still cannot see the market taking it very badly because the previous month was so weak," Garvey said.
He suggested people may look a little more closely this time at the mortgage numbers.

"We are expecting a slight acceleration in residential mortgage growth. It is currently running at 16.5 percent we expect to go up to 16.7 percent. That means the housing market is still very strong but we would expect that number to start peaking out over the next few months," Garvey said.
NCB's King said he expected central bank reserves to be considerably down due to the degree of intervention to support the Irish pound exchange rate versus sterling.

The Irish pound recently dropped below parity against sterling for the first time in 18 months after a bullish run on the British currency sparked by expectations of further interest rate increases in Britain.

"On the reserves front we do expect a significant fall because there has been heavy intervention to support the sterling/Irish (exchange rate) at close to one-for-one," King said. "So we have a fall of 500 million punts pencilled in and we think that might not even be enough."
King is forecasting central bank reserves at 5.2 billion punts at end-October, down from 5.7 billion. "But it could be lower," he said.
